nameStory: Bothropolys multidentatus gets its name from the Greek 'bothros' meaning pit or groove, and 'polys' meaning many, referring to the grooved segments of its body. The species name 'multidentatus' means 'many-toothed,' describing the numerous sharp projections on its forcipules (poison claws). Scientists gave it this technical name because common names for specific centipede species are rare - most people simply call them all 'centipedes'!
description: This is a stone centipede, a fast-moving predator with a flattened, segmented body that's perfectly designed for squeezing under rocks and logs. It has exactly 15 pairs of long, spindly legs that give it surprising speed when disturbed. Adults typically reach about 1-1.5 inches long, with a golden-brown to reddish-brown coloration. Like all centipedes, it's a hunter that uses venomous front claws to capture small insects, spiders, and other tiny creatures.

idTips.label: Leg count
idTips.description: Always has exactly 15 pairs of legs (30 total) - count carefully as this separates it from millipedes which have many more, and other centipede families with different leg counts

idTips.label: Body shape
idTips.description: Distinctly flattened from top to bottom, like it's been gently pressed - you can feel this if you gently touch it with a stick or leaf

idTips.label: Speed and movement
idTips.description: Moves with startling quickness when exposed, darting in zigzag patterns rather than straight lines - much faster than millipedes

idTips.label: Coloration
idTips.description: Golden-brown to rusty reddish-brown with slightly darker banding across segments - has a subtle metallic sheen in good light

idTips.label: Antennae
idTips.description: Long, thread-like antennae that are constantly moving and tapping - much longer relative to body size than millipede antennae

idTips.label: Forcipules
idTips.description: Front 'legs' are actually modified into claw-like poison fangs that curve forward under the head - visible as darker, thicker appendages

habitat: Look for this centipede under stones, rotting logs, and leaf litter in deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England. It prefers moist but well-drained areas with loose, organic soil where it can hunt for small prey. You'll often find it in the same spots where you might discover salamanders or ground beetles - anywhere that stays consistently damp but doesn't flood.

seasonality.spring: Becomes active as soil warms, often found under stones and logs during garden cleanup. This is when they're easiest to spot as they haven't yet established deep summer hideouts.
seasonality.summer: Most active at night but can be found during day under cover objects. Peak hunting season when prey is abundant - look for them under stones in shaded areas.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to move deeper into soil and under larger logs. Often encountered when raking leaves or moving firewood.
seasonality.winter: Hibernates deep in soil or under large logs and rocks below the frost line. Rarely seen unless you're doing major digging or construction work.

funFact: Despite being called a centipede (meaning '100 feet'), this species has exactly 30 legs its entire adult life - and amazingly, if it loses a leg to a predator, it can regenerate a perfect replacement when it molts, complete with all the joints and sensory structures!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with house centipedes (which have much longer, more delicate legs) and millipedes (which curl up when threatened and move slowly). Remember: centipedes are fast and flat, millipedes are slow and cylindrical. If it races away when you lift a rock, it's probably a centipede!
contextualKnowledge: Many people fear centipedes, but this species is far too small to bite humans effectively, and they're actually beneficial predators that help control pest insects. The 'hundred-legger' nickname is misleading since no centipede actually has 100 legs - they always have an odd number of leg pairs.
compareHints: Since this is the only Bothropolys species regularly found in New England, compare it to other stone centipedes in the Lithobiidae family by counting legs carefully - some relatives have fewer leg pairs. It's distinguished from house centipedes by its shorter, sturdier legs and preference for outdoor habitats rather than basements and bathrooms. The flattened body separates it immediately from the more cylindrical soil centipedes you might find in compost piles.
